title: Remember me (Luke 23:32–43)
hookLine: a dying thief asks to be remembered and is promised paradise today

lines: TWO MEN, TWO VERY DIFFERENT WORDS.
cards: A hill outside the city walls, called the place of the skull. Calvary, in the old Latin. Three crosses: Jesus in the middle, a criminal on each side.
The crowd watches. Soldiers cast lots for his clothes. And the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross, in the Douay-Rheims, is this: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do."
Then the men beside him start talking. One joins the mocking: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us.
And the other, who has nothing left, no time, no chance to make anything right, turns his head and says something nobody expects.

teach.b: He tells the first man to stop. We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then, to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom."
No speech. No list of what he did. Notice what he calls the man dying next to him: Lord.

And what he asks for: not to be taken down from the cross, only to be remembered. Jesus answers: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Paradise is a Persian word that came into Greek.

It first meant a walled garden, the kind a king kept. Jewish writers used it for the garden of Eden, and then for the place where God keeps the righteous. So a man dying on a cross is promised a garden, and not someday.
This day. Luke never gives his name.

Later Christian writings call him Dismas, and Catholics know him as the good thief, honored as a saint; some ask his prayers for the dying and for prisoners. Look at what the text leaves out. No baptism is mentioned.
No time to make amends, no list of sins, no promise to do better.

teach.h: ONE HONEST SENTENCE AT THE END.
teach.b: One honest sentence, at the very end.

teach.h: THIS DAY THOU SHALT BE WITH ME IN PARADISE.
teach.b: The Church reads this story as a sign that mercy can reach anyone, right up to the last breath.

how: Catholics hear the good thief's words in the Passion on Good Friday, and many ask Saint Dismas to pray for the dying and for people in prison.

o: Peter's plea after he denied knowing Jesus
the words Jesus said over the bread at supper
a dying thief's plea, with nothing to offer

games.q: who said what on the hill — tap the pairs.

s: the Gospel gives the good thief's name
Luke never names him. Dismas comes from later Christian writings.
paradise first meant a walled garden
a Persian word for a king's enclosed garden, taken into Greek.
the good thief lists everything he did wrong
he says one sentence: Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom.

games.q: you're the second criminal, dying beside Jesus, with no time left to fix anything. what do you say?
games.why: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." and he is promised paradise, this day.

practice: No long list, no explaining yourself: just notice what it's like to want to be remembered, by someone you love, or by God, and let the wanting be there without dressing it up.
If you pray, you can use the thief's own words, slowly, a few times: Lord, remember me. If you don't, you can just hold the wish quietly and breathe.

wordCard.voice: Remember me. What a dying thief asked for, with nothing to offer, and the answer he got: today. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, from a Persian word for a walled garden: the king's park, then Eden, then the place of the blessed.

carryVoice: Your line: this day in paradise. He asked only to be remembered. That's day sixty-four.
